tagline: Generate branded icon and illustration sets locally with ComfyUI, then organize the results.
verdictSummary: A local ComfyUI setup with a vector-friendly diffusion model can generate icon and illustration sets, and a prompt library on top of it keeps runs organized and reproducible. What it cannot do is Recraft's actual differentiator: a model specifically trained to output clean, editable vector paths rather than a raster image traced into vectors, plus a matching style system that keeps a whole icon set visually consistent.
coreLoopDIY: Write a prompt with style and reference-image controls, submit it to a local ComfyUI instance running an open vector-style diffusion workflow, save the exact parameters beside every output, and browse past generations in a searchable contact sheet.
whatYouLose: a model trained specifically for clean, editable vector output rather than raster-to-vector tracing
Recraft's style-consistency system across a whole generated set
hosted GPU capacity, so generation doesn't queue behind your own hardware
a licensed, curated training dataset behind the model
mobile and web access without a machine running locally
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for Recraft because generating a raster image is the easy part — training a model that reliably outputs clean vector paths instead of a traced bitmap, and keeps a whole set of icons visually consistent, is the actual product. A local ComfyUI workflow generates raster images; getting genuinely vector output at that quality needs the model Recraft built, not a prompt box in front of a general-purpose one.
prompt:
Build a local image-generation workflow manager: a prompt library and job queue in front of a self-hosted ComfyUI instance, for producing and organizing sets of branded assets. Do not build a new diffusion model or attempt to match Recraft's proprietary vector-output model — this wraps whatever open model the user installs in ComfyUI.

Core loop: the user writes a prompt with a negative prompt, seed, dimensions, and a chosen ComfyUI workflow (an installed model + settings preset), submits it to a local ComfyUI server, and the job queue polls for completion. Every output is saved to disk with a sidecar JSON file recording the exact prompt, seed, and workflow used, so any result can be reproduced exactly. A contact-sheet view lets the user browse, favorite, tag, and re-run past generations, and supports local image-to-image (feeding a saved output back in as a reference) without uploading anything anywhere.

This needs ComfyUI installed and running locally — either on a machine with a capable GPU, or pointed at a self-managed remote GPU box the user rents. No cloud API key is required if the user supplies their own model files with an appropriate license; without a GPU, generation is simply slow or impractical, and the README should say so rather than silently degrading.

Do not build: a new frontier diffusion model, a hosted generation service other people can use, or a claim that outputs are true vector paths — ComfyUI's standard workflows produce raster images. If the user wants an SVG, the honest scope is tracing a raster output afterward with a separate tool, not the model itself.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Recraft projects?
faq.a: No — Recraft's generation history and style presets live on their servers and aren't exportable in a form this build can read. You'd start a fresh prompt library from your first local generation.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: Only as a client to a machine running ComfyUI elsewhere on your network. The generation itself needs a GPU, which phones don't have; you're browsing and queuing jobs, not rendering on-device.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing per generation if you own the GPU — electricity aside. Renting cloud GPU time instead runs roughly $0.50–$2 per hour depending on the card, billed only while a job is actually running.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: True vector output. Recraft's model was trained to produce clean, editable paths; a standard local diffusion model produces a raster image, and turning that into a vector afterward with a tracing tool never looks as clean as output from a model built for it.
